content: The consolidated guidelines on HIV prevention, testing, treatment, service delivery, and monitoring emphasize the importance of addressing co-infections and comorbidities, particularly visceral leishmaniasis and cervical cancer, in people living with HIV. Below is a detailed explanation of the key points: Visceral Leishmaniasis and HIV Co-Infection Visceral leishmaniasis (VL) is a significant opportunistic infection in individuals with HIV, particularly in endemic regions. The two diseases exacerbate each other, with HIV increasing susceptibility to VL and VL accelerating HIV replication and disease progression. People with HIV are 100 to 2320 times more likely to develop active VL compared to the general population. In endemic areas, many individuals have asymptomatic VL infections, and as of now, 42 countries have reported cases of HIV and VL co-infection since the first case in 1985. In southern Europe, up to 70% of adult VL cases are associated with HIV, although the incidence has declined due to improved access to antiretroviral therapy (ART). However, in regions with limited ART access or where VL occurs in advanced HIV disease, co-infection rates are rising. The clinical presentation of VL in people with HIV is often atypical, involving various organs such as the gastrointestinal tract, lungs, and skin, especially in those with advanced HIV and low CD4 counts. Co-infections with other opportunistic pathogens are common, complicating early diagnosis. Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) has been reported in individuals with latent or treated VL who initiate ART. Diagnosis of VL relies on parasitological tests (e.g., bone marrow or spleen aspirates) and serological tests (e.g., ELISA, rK39, or PCR). However, diagnostic tests perform less effectively in HIV-VL co-infected individuals due to lower sensitivity and specificity. Parasite loads are higher in these patients, and parasites may be found in unusual sites. Treatment recommendations from the WHO include a combination of liposomal amphotericin B and miltefosine to improve efficacy and reduce toxicity. Secondary prophylaxis is advised after the first VL episode to prevent relapse. Optimal management aims to cure VL and achieve undetectable HIV viral loads through rapid ART initiation. For pregnant women, amphotericin B is the preferred treatment, as miltefosine is teratogenic and should not be used during pregnancy. Cervical Cancer and HIV Cervical cancer is the fourth most common cancer among women worldwide, with over half a million new cases annually. It is preventable and treatable, yet more than 311,000 women die from it each year, with 87% of deaths occurring in lowand middle-income countries. Women living with HIV are six times more likely to develop cervical cancer than those without HIV, as HIV increases susceptibility to HPV infection, reduces regression of precancerous lesions, accelerates progression to cancer, and raises recurrence rates after treatment. Cervical cancer is classified as an AIDS-defining condition. The WHO has set 2030 targets to eliminate cervical cancer as a public health problem, including vaccinating 90% of girls with the HPV vaccine by age 15, screening 70% of women with a high-performance test by ages 35 and 45, and ensuring 90% of women with cervical disease receive treatment. Updated WHO guidelines recommend HPV DNA testing as the primary screening method for women living with HIV, starting at age 25. Screening intervals of 3–5 years are suggested, with screening continuing until two consecutive negative results after age 50. HPV vaccination is recommended for girls aged 9–14 before sexual activity begins, with a three-dose schedule for immunocompromised individuals, including those living with HIV. Cardiovascular Disease and HIV People living with HIV have an increased risk of developing cardiovascular diseases (CVD) compared to the general population. This risk is influenced by chronic immune activation, inflammation, ART-related side effects, and traditional CVD risk factors. Studies show a 40–70% higher risk of myocardial infarction and cerebrovascular disease in people with HIV, even among those on ART. ART, while beneficial in reducing HIV-related morbidity and mortality, may contribute to lipid abnormalities and increased CVD risk, particularly with certain drug classes like protease inhibitors (PIs) and some nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs). CVD screening is recommended for people living with HIV, focusing on modifiable risk factors such as hypertension, smoking, obesity, and unhealthy diets. General Recommendations The WHO emphasizes the integration of HIV care with the management of non-communicable diseases (NCDs) to address the growing burden of chronic conditions in people living with HIV. This includes routine screening for NCDs, such as diabetes, hypertension, and cancers, as part of primary care. Comprehensive care should also include nutritional support, access to contraception, and pregnancy testing for women of childbearing age before administering teratogenic drugs like miltefosine. In summary, the WHO guidelines highlight the importance of addressing co-infections, comorbidities, and NCDs in people living with HIV through integrated care, early diagnosis, and effective treatment strategies.
